# Strict depth interpolation with one integer coordinate This is a theorem for n=1 and arbitrary d>=1, using mixed d-volume. It does not assert its counterpart with several integer coordinates, and does not prove OC. Let C subset R x R^d be compact and convex, and let mu(A)=sum_(z in Z) vol_d({x:(z,x) in C intersect A}). Assume 00. Then, for every integer p strictly between z_0 and z_1, the point y=(p,x)=(1-t)y_0+t y_1, t=(p-z_0)/(z_1-z_0), satisfies D(y)>min{D(y_0),D(y_1)}. (1) In particular, two distinct global mixed-depth maximizing bases must be adjacent. Same-parity distinct maximizing bases are impossible. The strict assertion concerns each fixed body and fixed pair; no uniform positive improvement in (1) is claimed. ## 1. Positive depth forces a fiber-interior point Write P={z:|C_z|>0}. It is a nonempty finite consecutive set of integers: Minkowski interpolation of two positive-volume fibers has positive volume at every intervening integer. Fibers of zero d-volume carry no mu mass and may be omitted from all sums. If x_0 is on the boundary of a positive-volume fiber C_(z_0), choose a nonzero supporting functional u with u.x_0=h_(z_0), where h_z=max_(C_z) u.x for z in P. Convexity implies h_w >= sum_j t_j h_(z_j) whenever w in P, t_j>=0, sum t_j=1, and sum t_j z_j=w. The finite linear program maximizing sum t_j h_(z_j) subject to the last two constraints at w=z_0 therefore has value h_(z_0). Finite-dimensional linear-program duality supplies an affine majorant a z+b>=h_z on P, with equality at z_0. Equivalently one may take a supporting affine piece of the finite concave polygonal roof of these data. The closed halfspace {u.x-a z>=b} contains (z_0,x_0). On each positive fiber it meets C_z only on a hyperplane, or not at all. Its mu mass is zero because u is nonzero and d>=1. Thus D(z_0,x_0)=0. Consequently every point in the theorem lies in the interior of its own fiber. The intermediate point y does as well: its fiber contains (1-t)C_(z_0)+t C_(z_1), and strict convex combinations of the two interior points contain a ball about x. This also proves directly that its fiber has positive volume. ## 2. A finite nonvertical cap attains depth at an integer base At y=(p,x) with integer p and positive-volume fiber, it is enough to consider through-y caps with nonzero continuous normal. Normalize that normal to |u|=1 and write the cap as H(a,u;y)={ (z,X): a(z-p)+u.(X-x)>=0 }. (2) Choose R with |X-x|<=R for all positive-volume fibers. If a>R+1, every fiber z>p is wholly captured and every fiber z

0. Halfspace depth is quasiconcave: a halfspace containing a convex combination of two points contains at least one of them, so D(y)>=alpha. Suppose equality holds and choose an attaining cap H at y as in (2). Its affine margin averages to zero between y_0 and y_1. If that margin is positive at an endpoint, translating its boundary parallel through that endpoint strictly decreases mu(H): a positive-volume slab of that endpoint's own fiber is removed, because the endpoint is interior to that fiber and the continuous normal is nonzero. This would give the endpoint a containing cap of mass strictly below alpha M. Therefore both endpoint margins are zero. The SAME cap H passes through y_0 and y_1, and has mass alpha M at both. It is consequently a minimizing cap at both endpoints. ## 4. Section weights and all supporting-facet possibilities Discard zero-volume fibers, and replace C by its intersection with the closed integer-base interval [min P,max P]. This preserves every mu integral and every positive fiber. There are at least three positive fibers here. Denote the section of this truncated C by the boundary hyperplane of H by E. Use |u|=1 and write its equation as u.X=b-a z. For each integer z put s_z=vol_(d-1){X in C_z:u.X=b-a z} (d>=2), s_z=1 if this section is nonempty, and 0 otherwise (d=1). In the d=1 formula a singleton has H_0 mass one. The common coarea factor 1/|u| is one; no ambient section Jacobian is inserted into s_z. Coordinates (z,xi) -> (z,xi+(b-a z)u), xi in u-perp, identify E with a convex set. Hence, for d>=2, Brunn--Minkowski makes s_z^(1/(d-1)) concave on its real positive-section interval. In particular its positive sampled values form a log-concave sequence at consecutive integer indices. For d=1 these positive sampled values are all one, so the same log-concavity conclusion holds. Every integer strictly inside the real projection of E has a PROPER cut through its full-dimensional fiber. Here is an explicit check of this qualification. The functions lower(z)=min_(C_z) [u.X+a z-b], upper(z)=max_(C_z) [u.X+a z-b] are respectively convex and concave on the real base interval. At the intermediate fiber p, lower(p)<0=0. Convexity/concavity then give lower(q)<0=2 have no effect on what follows. It follows that among the positive s_z, all but possibly the first and last correspond to proper cuts. The same is true for d=1. If an extreme section is proper, its weight also remains compulsory below. For a fixed endpoint y_e=(z_e,x_e), vary the integer tilt in (2) while pivoting the cap about y_e, keeping u fixed. Since H is minimizing there, the resulting scalar cap-mass function has a local minimum at the original tilt a. At a proper section its derivative contribution is (z-z_e)s_z. At a supporting section its two one-sided contributions are 0 and (z-z_e)s_z, in the appropriate order. At a fiber not meeting the plane both contributions are zero. These statements follow by integrating the one-dimensional section density in the direction u; it is continuous at a proper cut and has its one-sided endpoint value at a supporting cut. They also hold for an interval when d=1. For completeness, the endpoint value agrees with the one-sided limit: compactness puts any limiting slice inside the endpoint section, while convex interpolation of that section with one interior point supplies scaled copies in nearby interior slices. Their (d-1)-volumes converge to the endpoint section's volume. If that volume is zero, the same compactness bound gives limit zero. The left derivative is nonpositive and the right derivative is nonnegative at a local minimum. Interpolating these two derivatives therefore supplies effective weights s'_z with s'_z=s_z at every proper cut, 0<=s'_z<=s_z at a supporting cut, sum_z (z-z_e)s'_z=0. (3) Thus z_e is a centroid of the positive section sequence with only its two extreme weights allowed to decrease. The total effective weight is positive: in particular the sections at z_0,z_1 and every index between them are proper and retain their positive weights. Notice that this argument does not assume differentiability at supporting facets, and it needs no arbitrary selection of a section centroid. ## 5. A log-concave sequence has a short endpoint-trimming mean interval Let w_0,...,w_L be positive and log-concave, with L>=2. Keep every interior weight fixed and allow the weights at 0 and L independently to range between zero and their original values. Every resulting centroid lies in [m_-,m_+], where m_- = sum_(i=0)^(L-1) i w_i / sum_(i=0)^(L-1) w_i, m_+ = sum_(i=1)^L i w_i / sum_(i=1)^L w_i. Indeed adding mass at the smallest index lowers the mean, and adding mass at the largest index raises it. We claim m_+-m_- <= 1. (4) Compare two probability sequences on {0,...,L-1}, proportional to w_i and to w_(i+1), respectively. Their likelihood ratio is proportional to w_(i+1)/w_i, which is nonincreasing by log-concavity. The second sequence consequently has no larger mean. Explicitly, if A=sum w_i, B=sum w_(i+1), their mean difference times AB equals sum_(i=2 because the section contains the two proper endpoint indices z_0=2 the section marginal is indexed by a multidimensional lattice. Aggregating it along a base direction need not give a log-concave sequence. In addition, optional supporting-section fibers can occupy many boundary indices. The one-dimensional endpoint-trimming argument therefore supplies no proof of strict parity interpolation in general n.

# Strict depth interpolation with one integer coordinate

This is a theorem for n=1 and arbitrary d>=1, using mixed d-volume.
It does not assert its counterpart with several integer coordinates,
and does not prove OC.

Let C subset R x R^d be compact and convex, and let

    mu(A)=sum_(z in Z) vol_d({x:(z,x) in C intersect A}).

Assume 0<M=mu(C)<infinity. For a point y define

    D(y)=inf_(closed halfspaces H containing y) mu(H)/M.

Let y_0=(z_0,x_0) and y_1=(z_1,x_1) belong to positive-volume fibers
of C, with z_0<z_1 integers. Suppose D(y_0),D(y_1)>0. Then, for every
integer p strictly between z_0 and z_1, the point

    y=(p,x)=(1-t)y_0+t y_1,  t=(p-z_0)/(z_1-z_0),

satisfies

    D(y)>min{D(y_0),D(y_1)}.                             (1)

In particular, two distinct global mixed-depth maximizing bases must
be adjacent. Same-parity distinct maximizing bases are impossible.
The strict assertion concerns each fixed body and fixed pair; no
uniform positive improvement in (1) is claimed.

Sections of the mathematical submission:
- 1. Positive depth forces a fiber-interior point
- 2. A finite nonvertical cap attains depth at an integer base
- 3. An equal-depth intermediate cap must pass through both endpoints
- 4. Section weights and all supporting-facet possibilities
- 5. A log-concave sequence has a short endpoint-trimming mean interval
- 6. Scope
